verdicts.reason: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/v261.2/man/loginctl.xml (primary source: the systemd project's own DocBook man page at the pinned v261.2 tag). Lines 186-195 define `enable-linger [USER…]` / `disable-linger [USER…]` and contain the quoted text verbatim: "If enabled for a specific user, a user manager is spawned for the user at boot and kept around after logouts. This allows users who are not logged in to run long-running services." Feature marked "Added in version 233", so it is current for v261.2. The freedesktop.org "latest" rendered page carries identical wording. Only nit (not a refutation): the USER argument is optional in the synopsis (`[USER…]`; defaults to the caller's session user, accepts names or numeric UIDs), whereas the claim writes it as a bare `USER`.

Fetched the cited primary source (HTTP 200, systemd repo tag v261.2, man/systemd.unit.xml, table "Load path when running in user mode (--user)"). Every path in the claim appears verbatim in that table: "$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user or $HOME/.config/systemd/user" with description "User configuration ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME is used if set, ~/.config otherwise)"; "$XDG_CONFIG_DIRS/systemd/user or /etc/xdg/systemd/user"; "/etc/systemd/user" (User units created by the administrator); "$XDG_DATA_HOME/systemd/user or $HOME/.local/share/systemd/user"; "/usr/local/lib/systemd/user" (User units installed by the administrator); "/usr/lib/systemd/user" (User units installed by the distribution package manager). The claim says "includes", so omitting the other entries (user.control, transient, generator dirs, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/systemd/user, /run/systemd/user, $XDG_DATA_DIRS/systemd/user, generator.late) is not a misstatement. The source is primary (upstream systemd docs at the pinned tag) and current for the stated version. No refutation found.

Fetched the cited primary source (HTTP 200, systemd repo tag v261.2, man/systemd.special.xml). Under refsect1 "Units managed by the user service manager" > "Special User Units", the default.target entry reads verbatim: "This is the main target of the user service manager, started by default when the service manager is invoked. Various services that compose the normal user session should be pulled into this target. In this regard, default.target is similar to multi-user.target in the system instance, but it is a real unit, not an alias." (version-info v242). The quotation in the claim is exact and correctly attributed to the user-manager section (not the system-manager default.target entry, which instead advises WantedBy= a regular target). The parenthetical inference "user services use WantedBy=default.target" is an interpretation, but it is directly supported by the source's statement that user-session services "should be pulled into this target" and by the contrast the source itself draws with the system instance. Source is primary, reachable, and version-matched; claim stands.

Fetched the cited primary source (systemd repo, tag v261.2, man/systemd.resource-control.xml; HTTP 200). The CPUQuota= entry reads verbatim: "Takes a percentage value, suffixed with "%". The percentage specifies how much CPU time the unit shall get at maximum, relative to the total CPU time available on one CPU. Use values > 100% for allotting CPU time on more than one CPU. This controls the cpu.max attribute on the unified control group hierarchy and cpu.cfs_quota_us on legacy." and "Example: CPUQuota=20% ensures that the executed processes will never get more than 20% CPU time on one CPU." (unified hierarchy = cgroup v2). The CPUWeight=/StartupCPUWeight= entry states the options "accept an integer value or the special string "idle"" and that "idle" marks the cgroup for idle scheduling, "which means that it will get CPU resources only when there are no processes not marked in this way to execute in this cgroup or its siblings. This setting corresponds to the cpu.idle cgroup attribute." (with a note it only has effect on cgroup-v2). Every quoted fragment matches the source at the stated version; the only looseness is the paraphrase "only when nothing else wants it", which the source scopes to non-idle processes in the same cgroup or its siblings — a simplification, not a contradiction. Source is primary and version-pinned.

Fetched the cited primary source (systemd repo at tag v261.2, man/systemd.resource-control.xml, HTTP 200). The MemoryMax= entry reads verbatim: "Specify the absolute limit on memory usage of the executed processes in this unit. If memory usage cannot be contained under the limit, out-of-memory killer is invoked inside the unit. It is recommended to use MemoryHigh= as the main control mechanism and use MemoryMax= as the last line of defense." The MemoryHigh= entry reads: "Specify the throttling limit on memory usage ... the processes are heavily slowed down and memory is taken away aggressively in such cases. This is the main mechanism to control memory usage of a unit." Both entries state: "If the value is suffixed with K, M, G or T, the specified memory size is parsed as Kilobytes, Megabytes, Gigabytes, or Terabytes (with the base 1024) ... Alternatively, a percentage value may be specified, which is taken relative to the installed physical memory on the system." Every quoted fragment and the suffix/percentage claim match the v261.2 source exactly; the source is primary (upstream systemd tree at the stated tag). Minor omission only: both settings also accept the special value "infinity", which the claim does not mention but does not contradict.

Fetched the cited primary source (HTTP 200, systemd upstream repo at tag v261.2, man/systemd.resource-control.xml; file contains v261 version-info markers, consistent with the stated version). Lines 624-631 of the IOWeight=/StartupIOWeight= entry read verbatim: "Takes a single weight value (between 1 and 10000) to set the default block I/O weight. This controls the io.weight control group attribute, which defaults to 100. For details about this control group attribute, see IO Interface Files. The available I/O bandwidth is split up among all units within one slice relative to their block I/O weight. A higher weight means more I/O bandwidth, a lower weight means less." The quoted claim matches the source exactly (the ellipsis elides only the kernel-docs cross-reference sentence). The source is primary (upstream systemd man page source) and current for v261.2; the setting is marked as added in v230 and not deprecated. Minor context the claim omits but does not contradict: the entry applies to the io controller in the unified (cgroup v2) hierarchy only.

Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/systemd/systemd/v261.2/man/systemctl.xml (HTTP 200, 162 KB, primary upstream source at the stated tag). The set-property entry (xml lines 674-707) reads verbatim: "Set the specified unit properties at runtime where this is supported. ... Not all properties may be changed at runtime, but many resource control settings (primarily those in systemd.resource-control(5)) may. The changes are applied immediately, and stored on disk for future boots, unless --runtime is passed, in which case the settings only apply until the next reboot." It includes the exact example "systemctl set-property foobar.service CPUWeight=200 MemoryMax=2G IPAccounting=yes" and "assigning an empty setting usually resets a property to its defaults" with example "systemctl set-property avahi-daemon.service IPAddressDeny=". The --runtime option text (line 2690) and the freedesktop.org /man/latest/systemctl.html page say the same. Only nit: the source qualifies the reset with "usually", which the claim's paraphrase omits; not material enough to refute.

Fetched the cited primary source (systemd upstream repo, tag v261.2, man/systemd-run.xml, HTTP 200, 41 KB) plus the xi:included man/user-system-options.xml at the same tag. Every element of the claim is present verbatim or in substance: (1) --property=/-p text at lines 140-143 reads exactly "Sets a property on the scope or service unit that is created. This option takes an assignment in the same format as systemctl(1)'s set-property command." (2) --scope (line 115-119): "Create a transient .scope unit instead of the default transient .service unit"; Description para: "If a command is run as transient scope unit, it will be executed by systemd-run itself as parent process ... Execution in this case is synchronous, and will return only when the command finishes. This mode is enabled via the --scope switch." (3) --user is included from user-system-options.xml: "Talk to the service manager of the calling user, rather than the service manager of the system." (= per-user manager); --slice= (lines 161-166): "Make the new .service or .scope unit part of the specified slice, instead of system.slice (when running in --system mode) or the root slice (when running in --user mode)." (4) Examples section contains literally "# systemd-run -p IOWeight=10 updatedb" (line 661) and "$ systemd-run --scope --user screen" (line 702). Source is primary, version matches v261.2, nothing outdated or misattributed.

Fetched the cited primary source (raw.githubusercontent.com systemd/systemd tag v261.2, units/user@.service.in; HTTP 200). Its [Service] section contains verbatim: "Slice=user-%i.slice", "KillMode=mixed", "Delegate=pids memory cpu", "DelegateSubgroup=init.scope". The Delegate= list names exactly pids, memory and cpu; "io" appears nowhere in the file, so the shipped template delegates only those three controllers by default. Cross-checked against /usr/lib/systemd/system/user@.service on the founder laptop (systemctl --version: systemd 261 (261.2-1-arch); pacman -Q: systemd 261.2-1): the four lines are byte-identical to the template (only the {{LIBEXECDIR}}/{{TimeoutStopSec}} placeholders are expanded). The claim is accurate for the stated version and the source is primary.

Source is primary and reachable: the v261.2 tag of units/user@.service.in contains "Delegate=pids memory cpu" (plus DelegateSubgroup=init.scope) — io is not in the delegated set, which is exactly why io.weight cannot appear under user@1000.service. Independently re-ran the test on the founder laptop (systemd 261 (261.2-1-arch), /sys/fs/cgroup is cgroup2fs; root cgroup.controllers includes io): `systemd-run --user --scope -p CPUQuota=20% -p MemoryMax=100M -p IOWeight=10 -- sh -c ...` landed in /user.slice/user-1000.slice/user@1000.service/app.slice/<unit>.scope with cgroup.controllers="cpu memory pids", cpu.max="20000 100000", memory.max=104857600, and no io.weight file (only io.pressure present); `systemctl show user@1000.service -p DelegateControllers` = "cpu memory pids"; `systemctl --user show <unit>.scope` still reports IOWeight=10 as a configured property and no warning was emitted on stderr or in the user journal, so "silently ineffective" is accurate. Claim matches source and reproduces as stated.

Fetched https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.html (HTTP 200, page blurb shows docs version 7.2.0 = kernel.org "latest" on 2026-08-22; this is the authoritative rendering of Documentation/admin-guide/cgroup-v2.rst, i.e. primary). Every element of the claim is supported verbatim: cpu.max is "A read-write two value file which exists on non-root cgroups. The default is 'max 100000'... format: $MAX $PERIOD"; memory.max reads "Memory usage hard limit. This is the main mechanism to limit memory usage of a cgroup. If a cgroup's memory usage reaches this limit and can't be reduced, the OOM killer is invoked in the cgroup." (the claim's ellipsis correctly elides one sentence); io.weight: "The default is 'default 100'... The weights are in the range [1, 10000]"; controller sections present are CPU, Memory, IO, PID, Cpuset, Device controller, RDMA, DMEM, HugeTLB, Misc; Device controller text: "Cgroup v2 device controller has no interface files and is implemented on top of cgroup BPF"; DMEM text: "The 'dmem' controller regulates the distribution and accounting of device memory regions" with "An example for xe follows: drm/0000:03:00.0/vram0 ..."; the only GPU-related strings on the page are those dmem xe/vram examples — no GPU-time/compute controller is documented. Minor nit (not a refutation): the page also documents perf_event under "Others" as a utility controller auto-enabled on v2 (and threaded); the claim's list omits it but does not assert exhaustiveness and perf_event is not a resource-distribution controller.

Fetched the cited primary source (systemd repo tag v261.2 confirmed: meson.version = 261.2) via curl. man/org.freedesktop.login1.xml contains verbatim: Manager section "The IdleHint property reflects the idle hint state of the system." (line 821); "IdleSinceHint and IdleSinceHintMonotonic encode the timestamps of the last change of the idle hint boolean, in CLOCK_REALTIME and CLOCK_MONOTONIC timestamps, respectively" (line 824); Session interface lists "SetIdleHint(in b idle);" (line 1208) and says "SetIdleHint() is called by the session object to update the idle state of the session whenever it changes." (line 1409); Session "CanIdle indicates whether the session supports the idle hint concept" (line 1600). man/logind.conf.xml at the same tag, IdleAction= entry (lines 149-162): "Note that this requires that user sessions correctly report the idle status to the system. The system will execute the action after all sessions report that they are idle, no idle inhibitor lock is active, and subsequently, the time configured with IdleActionSec= ... has expired." The inferential clause "logind does not measure graphical idleness itself" is corroborated by a second primary source at the same tag, src/login/logind-session.c session_get_idle_hint() (line 1160ff): "/* Graphical sessions have an explicit idle hint */ if (SESSION_TYPE_IS_GRAPHICAL(s->type)) ... return s->idle_hint;" — logind only does its own measurement (tty atime) for SESSION_TTY sessions, never for graphical ones. Minor precision note (not a refutation): logind does measure idleness for TTY sessions via tty atime; the claim is correctly scoped to graphical idleness.

Fetched the cited file at tag 50.1 (881 lines of C, GNOME's official GitHub mirror of gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/gnome-session). Lines 452-476 define gsm_systemd_set_session_idle(), which emits g_debug("Updating systemd idle status: %d", is_idle) and then g_dbus_connection_call(bus, SD_NAME="org.freedesktop.login1", manager->priv->session_path, SD_SESSION_INTERFACE="org.freedesktop.login1.Session", "SetIdleHint", g_variant_new("(b)", is_idle), ...). Line 831 installs it in the GsmSystem vtable. Cross-checked that it is actually wired in 50.1: gsm-manager.c lines 1302-1311 (on_presence_status_changed) call gsm_system_set_session_idle(system, status == GSM_PRESENCE_STATUS_IDLE), and gsm-presence.c drives that status from GnomeIdleMonitor idle/active watches (lines 170-206), with gsm-presence.c still in meson.build. Claim and verbatim string both match; the inference that loginctl's IdleHint is meaningful on GNOME is supported. Minor caveats (not refutations): the hint follows GNOME's idle-delay timeout, is suppressed while idle is inhibited (gsm-manager.c update_idle), and is skipped with a warning if no logind session path exists.

Cited source is primary (KDE's own GitLab, raw file at signed tag v6.7.4 — tag existence confirmed via invent.kde.org API, target 7a685f9c). interface.cpp at v6.7.4 lines 123-130 read exactly as claimed: `uint Interface::GetSessionIdleTime() { if (KWindowSystem::isPlatformWayland()) { QDBusContext::sendErrorReply(QDBusError::NotSupported, QStringLiteral("GetSessionIdleTime is not supported on this platform")); return 0; } return KIdleTime::instance()->idleTime(); }`. GetActive (line 113, returns lockState()==Locked) and GetActiveTime (line 118, returns m_daemon->activeTime()) have no Wayland guard. interface.h line 50 binds the class to D-Bus interface "org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver" and dbus/org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver.xml at the same tag lists GetActive/GetActiveTime/GetSessionIdleTime. The local-reproduction part also checks out on this machine: XDG_SESSION_TYPE=wayland, pacman reports kscreenlocker 6.7.4-1, and `busctl --user call org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver /ScreenSaver org.freedesktop.ScreenSaver GetSessionIdleTime` returns "Call failed: GetSessionIdleTime is not supported on this platform" while GetActive returns `b false` and GetActiveTime returns `u 0`. Claim stands as written for the stated version. (Minor non-refuting note: KIdleTime::idleTime() is in milliseconds, whereas the freedesktop ScreenSaver spec documents seconds; the claim makes no unit assertion, so this does not affect it.)

Fetched the cited primary source (mutter tag 50.4, data/dbus-interfaces/org.gnome.Mutter.IdleMonitor.xml, HTTP 200). It contains the verbatim description "This interface is used by gnome-desktop to implement user activity monitoring", and defines GetIdletime (out idletime:t), AddIdleWatch (in interval:t, documented "Interval, in milliseconds"; out id:u), AddUserActiveWatch (out id:u), RemoveWatch (in id:u), ResetIdletime, and signal WatchFired (id:u). The XML itself does not state the object path; I verified it against mutter 50.4 src/backends/meta-idle-manager.c, which exports the skeleton at "/org/gnome/Mutter/IdleMonitor/Core" under object manager "/org/gnome/Mutter/IdleMonitor" and owns bus name "org.gnome.Mutter.IdleMonitor". For gnome-shell 50.4, data/dbus-interfaces/org.gnome.ScreenSaver.xml (HTTP 200) defines Lock, GetActive (out b), SetActive (in b), GetActiveTime (out u), signal ActiveChanged (b), signal WakeUpScreen; js/ui/shellDBus.js exports it at /org/gnome/ScreenSaver and GetActive returns screenShield.active. One precision caveat, not a refutation: GetActive/ActiveChanged report the screen shield's *active* state, which is distinct from the shield's separate `locked` property (gnome-shell screenShield.js keeps _isActive and _isLocked separately; lock state is not exposed on this interface). The parenthetical "(lock state)" is therefore a loose gloss; active implies locked only when the lock setting is enabled. Both 50.4 tags resolved via raw.githubusercontent.com, so the claim is current for the stated version.
verdicts.corrected_statement: GNOME/Mutter 50.4 exposes org.gnome.Mutter.IdleMonitor ("used by gnome-desktop to implement user activity monitoring") on the session bus at object path /org/gnome/Mutter/IdleMonitor/Core, with GetIdletime() -> t, AddIdleWatch(interval: t, milliseconds) -> id: u (fires signal WatchFired(id: u) repeatedly), AddUserActiveWatch() -> id: u (fires once), RemoveWatch(id: u), and ResetIdletime(). gnome-shell 50.4 also exports org.gnome.ScreenSaver at /org/gnome/ScreenSaver with Lock, GetActive -> b, SetActive(b), GetActiveTime -> u, and signals ActiveChanged(b) and WakeUpScreen; GetActive/ActiveChanged reflect the screen shield's active state (screensaver/shield up), which coincides with "locked" only when screen locking is enabled — the shield's separate locked flag is not exposed on this interface.

verdicts.reason: Fetched the primary source at the exact tag (gitlab.freedesktop.org raw, ref 1.45; tag 1.45 exists, commit 0091197f "build: Bump version to 1.45", 2025-06-13; meson.build version: '1.45'). The file staging/ext-idle-notify/ext-idle-notify-v1.xml confirms every element of the claim: copyright "© 2015 Martin Gräßlin / © 2022 Simon Ser" under an MIT/X11 permission notice; interface ext_idle_notifier_v1 version="2" with request get_idle_notification(id new_id ext_idle_notification_v1, timeout uint "minimum idle timeout in msec", seat wl_seat); ext_idle_notification_v1 sends an idled event "when no user activity has happened for at least the timeout duration" and a resumed event "when user activity starts again"; and the since="2" request get_input_idle_notification whose description says "it ignores idle inhibitors" and that "only input from the user, e.g. from a keyboard or mouse, counts as activity". The protocol lives under staging/ as claimed. Only trivial wording differences (source says "at least the timeout"; "e.g. keyboard or mouse" rather than strictly "only keyboard/mouse"), none material.

research.dossier:
DOSSIER R06 — Coordinator & schema (CORVID). Verified 2026-08-22 against primary sources only (docs.docker.com / compose-spec repo / docker/compose v5.5.0 source, postgresql.org docs for PG 18, docker-library postgres README + official-images tag list, tailscale.com KB + tailscale/tailscale source at main commit 86e5d38, kubernetes.io source, kernel cgroup-v2 doc, Hadoop Fair Scheduler doc, the DRF NSDI'11 paper PDF, llama.cpp server README at master e85caa8). Hub context assumed: Ubuntu hub (solarplexus) running Docker, Tailscale in userspace mode; coordinator = Python + Postgres.

1) POSTGRES AS ITS OWN COMPOSE PROJECT
- Isolation: Compose isolates environments by project name; precedence is -p flag > COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME > top-level `name:` > directory name (F6). So `name: corvid-db` in its own directory is a first-class separate project; the obsolete `version:` key should be omitted (F6).
- Resource caps: both styles are honored by `docker compose` v5.5.0 — service-level `cpus`/`mem_limit`/`mem_reservation`/`cpu_shares`/`pids_limit` AND `deploy.resources.limits.{cpus,memory,pids}` / `reservations.{memory,devices}` are mapped onto the container HostConfig in pkg/compose/create.go (F1–F3). Code comment: "Cpu reservation is a swarm option and PIDs is only a limit" — i.e. `reservations.cpus` is ignored outside Swarm (F2). Spec requires `cpus` and `deploy.cpus` to agree if both set (F3). Docker resource docs: `--memory` minimum 6m; `--cpu-shares` default 1024 is a soft weight only enforced under contention (F14).
- Data dir: for the postgres image 18+, PGDATA is /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker and the declared VOLUME moved to /var/lib/postgresql — mount there; for ≤17 mount /var/lib/postgresql/data (mounting /var/lib/postgresql on ≤17 WILL NOT persist) (F7). Bind-mount long syntax: type: bind, source, target, read_only, bind.create_host_path (default true); relative host paths resolve from the Compose file's directory (F5). Arbitrary --user works if PGDATA owner matches; initdb needs the UID in /etc/passwd (bind-mount /etc/passwd:ro) (F13).
- Shared memory: container /dev/shm defaults to 64MB; image README's own compose example sets `shm_size: 128mb` and suggests --shm-size=256MB (F8).
- Healthcheck: compose fields test/interval/timeout/retries/start_period/start_interval; `depends_on: {db: {condition: service_healthy}}` is guaranteed healthy-before-start (F4). pg_isready exit 0 = accepting, 1 = rejecting (startup), 2 = no response, 3 = bad params; wrong creds still work but log a failed attempt — so pass the real -U/-d (F12).
- Init: /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d scripts run only on an EMPTY data dir, as the postgres user; a failed script + orchestrator restart will NOT re-run them (F9). POSTGRES_PASSWORD is mandatory (F7).
- Version pin: current official tags include 18.6, 18.6-trixie, 18.6-alpine, 17.11 (F10); PG 18 supported until 2030-11-14, PG 17 until 2029-11-08 (F11). PostgreSQL License is BSD/MIT-like (F39); the image's Dockerfiles are MIT (F40).

2) QUEUE PATTERN (SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
- PG 18 docs: "With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped… can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table" (F15); with LIMIT, locking stops once enough rows are returned, but OFFSET-skipped rows DO get locked (F16). Feature since 9.5 (Thomas Munro) (F17).
- Companion primitives: LISTEN/NOTIFY payload <8000 bytes, delivered only on commit; docs recommend putting data in a table and sending only the key, ideally from a statement trigger (F18) — this is exactly "poll + wake-up" for a job table. Advisory locks exist (session vs transaction level; pg_try_advisory_xact_lock non-blocking) but are NOT needed for the claim query and are dangerous with LIMIT (F19). Partial index `WHERE state='queued'` keeps the hot index tiny (F20). Heartbeat upsert: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE is atomic insert-or-update and can reference EXCLUDED (F21). now()/CURRENT_TIMESTAMP is transaction start time; clock_timestamp() is wall-clock (F22). timestamptz is stored as UTC; bare `timestamp` is "without time zone" and silently drops zone info — always use timestamptz (F23).

3) HEARTBEAT / ROSTER PATTERNS (design reference, not a dependency)
- Kubernetes: two heartbeat forms (Node .status every 5 min by default; lightweight Lease renewed every 10 s by default; unreachable timeout 40 s; retry backoff 200 ms→7 s cap; controller checks every 5 s; 5 min more before eviction) (F24). A heartbeat is literally an update of Lease.spec.renewTime and the control plane judges availability from that timestamp (F25) — i.e. the "roster row + last_seen column" pattern, sanctioned at planet scale.

4) FAIR-SHARE WHEN CONTENDED, NO QUOTAS (max-min)
- Hadoop Fair Scheduler defines the behavior: "all apps get, on average, an equal share of resources over time… When there is a single app running, that app uses the entire cluster… resources that free up are assigned to the new apps", weights optional (F26). cgroup v2 formalizes "weights" (work-conserving, only active children participate, cpu.weight default 100, range 1–10000) vs "limits" (cpu.max, may be over-committed) (F27). DRF (Ghodsi et al., NSDI'11) notes round-robin, proportional sharing and weighted fair queueing all implement (weighted) max-min fairness and generalizes it to multi-resource (F28). Kubernetes APF uses per-flow fair queuing keyed by requesting user so one flood cannot starve others (F29). Net: a per-member round-robin (or DRR) at claim time = max-min fair, no quotas, full use when uncontended.

5) IDENTITY FROM TAILSCALE FOR THE API
- Tailscale Serve injects Tailscale-User-Login / -Name / -Profile-Pic into proxied HTTP, strips spoofed copies inbound, only for tailnet traffic (never Funnel), not for tagged devices, and the KB's best practice is that the backend listens on localhost only (F30).
- `tailscale whois ip[:port] [--json]` resolves Machine + User (email) + Capabilities (F31); the LocalAPI endpoint is GET /localapi/v0/whois?addr=IP[:port] → {Node, UserProfile, CapMap}, 404 on no match, gated by PermitRead (F32). On Linux tailscaled.sock is 0666 and any local unix-socket client gets read permission (F33), so a Python service can call it without root.
- BUT the hub runs userspace networking: tailscaled acts as a SOCKS5/HTTP proxy (F34) and netstack forwards inbound TCP to the node's Tailscale IP by dialing 127.0.0.1:<port> with a standard dialer (F35) — the backend's TCP peer address is loopback, so whois-on-IP cannot identify the caller there. Serve headers are therefore the identity mechanism on the hub. Serve-under-userspace is implied by the Docker image (TS_USERSPACE on by default + TS_SERVE_CONFIG) (F34) but is not stated for the bare-metal hub → spike (F36, unverified).

6) LOG POLICY (METADATA ONLY)
- Postgres defaults are already metadata-safe: log_statement=none, log_min_duration_statement=-1 (but when enabled, log_parameter_max_length=-1 logs bind params IN FULL), log_connections='' and log_disconnections=off (F37). Pin these explicitly so a future "debug" flip is a deliberate ADR-level act.
- llama-server: `--log-prompts-dir` is debug-only and disabled by default; `/slots` endpoint is ON by default (per-slot state incl. sampling params) → run `--no-slots`; `--metrics` (aggregate Prometheus) is off by default and is the metadata-friendly choice (F38).

7) LICENSES/TAGS VERIFIED: Docker Compose v5.5.0 Apache-2.0 (F41); psycopg 3.3.4 LGPL-3.0 (F42); tailscale v1.102.3 BSD-3-Clause (F43); FastAPI 0.141.1 MIT, uvicorn 0.52.4 BSD-3 as candidates (F44).

facts.statement: Compose Deploy Spec: `resources` has `limits` ("The platform must prevent the container to allocate more") and `reservations` ("The platform must guarantee the container can allocate at least the configured amount"); `cpus` = number of cores, `memory` = byte-value string, `pids` = integer; documented example uses limits cpus '0.50', memory 50M, pids 1 and reservations cpus '0.25', memory 20M. The page does not itself state whether non-Swarm Compose honors them.

docker compose v5.5.0 honors deploy.resources in non-Swarm mode: pkg/compose/create.go getDeployResources() maps service-level MemLimit/MemReservation/CPUShares/CPUS(NanoCPUs)/PidsLimit onto container.Resources, then setLimits() maps deploy.resources.limits.memory→Memory, limits.cpus→NanoCPUs, limits.pids→PidsLimit, and setReservations() maps reservations.memory→MemoryReservation and reservations.devices→DeviceRequests; code comment: "Cpu reservation is a swarm option and PIDs is only a limit" (reservations.cpus is ignored).

Compose service attributes: `cpus` "define the number of (potentially virtual) CPUs to allocate to service containers. This is a fractional number. 0.000 means no limit" and "When both are set, cpus must be consistent with the cpus attribute in the Deploy Specification"; `mem_limit` "configures a limit on the amount of memory a container can allocate" and must be consistent with deploy limits.memory; `mem_reservation` = memory reservation; `cpu_shares` = "relative CPU weight versus other containers"; `pids_limit` (-1 unlimited); `shm_size` configures /dev/shm size.

Compose `healthcheck` fields: test (string or list, e.g. ["CMD", ...]), interval, timeout, retries, start_period, start_interval (durations); example interval 1m30s / timeout 10s / retries 3 / start_period 40s / start_interval 5s. `depends_on` long syntax supports `condition: service_healthy` ("Compose guarantees dependency services marked with service_healthy are 'healthy' before starting a dependent service"), `service_started`, and `restart: true` (restart dependent after dependency updates); `restart` policies: no, always, on-failure[:max-retries], unless-stopped.

Compose `volumes`: short syntax VOLUME:CONTAINER_PATH[:ACCESS_MODE]; long syntax fields type (volume|bind|tmpfs|image|npipe|cluster), source (host path for bind), target, read_only, bind.propagation, bind.create_host_path ("Creates a directory at the source path on host if there is nothing present. Defaults to true"), bind.selinux; relative host paths resolve from the Compose file's parent directory and are only supported for local container runtimes.

Compose project names isolate environments; precedence (highest first): -p flag, COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME env, top-level `name:` attribute, base name of the project directory, base name of cwd; names must be lowercase letters/digits/dashes/underscores starting with a letter or digit. Top-level `version` is obsolete ("only informative and you'll receive a warning message that it is obsolete if used"); Compose always validates with the most recent schema.

postgres official image: POSTGRES_PASSWORD "is required for you to use the PostgreSQL image. It must not be empty or undefined"; for PostgreSQL 18+ PGDATA is version-specific ("For 18 it is /var/lib/postgresql/18/docker") and the declared VOLUME moved to /var/lib/postgresql — "Mounts and volumes should be targeted at the updated location"; for 17 and below "Mount the data volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data and not at /var/lib/postgresql because mounts at the latter path WILL NOT PERSIST database data when the container is re-created". Docker-specific env vars only take effect when the data directory is empty.

postgres official image: "the default /dev/shm size for containers is 64MB. If the shared memory is exhausted you will encounter ERROR: could not resize shared memory segment … No space left on device. You will want to pass --shm-size=256MB for example to docker run, or alternatively in docker compose"; the README's own compose example sets `shm_size: 128mb` (or a tmpfs mount at /dev/shm for swarm).

postgres official image: *.sql, *.sql.gz, *.sh under /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d run after initdb, in sorted name order, as the postgres user; "scripts in /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d are only run if you start the container with a data directory that is empty; any pre-existing database will be left untouched"; if a script fails and the orchestrator restarts the container with the already-initialized data dir, it will not continue with your scripts.

Current postgres official image tags include 18.6, 18, latest, 18.6-trixie, 18-trixie; 18.6-bookworm; 18.6-alpine3.24 / 18-alpine / alpine; 17.11, 17, 17.11-trixie, 17.11-bookworm, 17.11-alpine; plus 19beta3 variants.

PostgreSQL versioning policy: a major version is supported for 5 years after initial release. PG 18 first release 2025-09-25, final release 2030-11-14 (current minor 18.6); PG 17: 2024-09-26 → 2029-11-08 (17.11); PG 16: 2023-09-14 → 2028-11-09 (16.15).

pg_isready "returns 0 to the shell if the server is accepting connections normally, 1 if the server is rejecting connections (for example during startup), 2 if there was no response to the connection attempt, and 3 if no attempt was made"; -d dbname / -h host / -U username; "It is not necessary to supply correct user name, password, or database name values to obtain the server status; however, if incorrect values are provided, the server will log a failed connection attempt."

postgres official image supports arbitrary --user: "postgres doesn't care what UID it runs as (as long as the owner of PGDATA matches), but initdb does care (and needs the user to exist in /etc/passwd)"; documented workarounds include bind-mounting /etc/passwd read-only (--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro) or pre-chowning the volume to the UID.

Docker resource constraints: --memory minimum allowed value is 6m; --cpus caps CPU (e.g. --cpus="1.5" on a 2-CPU host = at most one and a half CPUs); --cpu-shares default 1024 is a relative weight that "is only enforced when CPU cycles are constrained" (a soft limit); "When you use these settings, Docker modifies the settings for the container's cgroup on the host machine."

SELECT locking clause: "With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work, but can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table." Grammar: FOR lock_strength [OF from_reference…] [NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED], lock_strength ∈ UPDATE | NO KEY UPDATE | SHARE | KEY SHARE; NOWAIT errors instead of waiting.
SELECT locking clause with LIMIT: "If a LIMIT is used, locking stops once enough rows have been returned to satisfy the limit (but note that rows skipped over by OFFSET will get locked)."
SKIP LOCKED was added in PostgreSQL 9.5: release note "Add SELECT option SKIP LOCKED to skip locked rows (Thomas Munro). This does not throw an error for locked rows like NOWAIT does."

NOTIFY: payload "In the default configuration it must be shorter than 8000 bytes. (If binary data or large amounts of information need to be communicated, it's best to put it in a database table and send the key of the record.)"; "if a NOTIFY is executed inside a transaction, the notify events are not delivered until and unless the transaction is committed"; recommended technique is to put the NOTIFY in a statement trigger on the table so notification happens automatically.

Advisory locks are application-defined locks the system does not enforce; session-level locks persist until released or session end and ignore transaction semantics, transaction-level locks auto-release at transaction end. pg_try_advisory_lock/pg_try_advisory_xact_lock return true/false without waiting; keys are one 64-bit or two 32-bit values. Warning: with ORDER BY/LIMIT, `SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100; -- danger!` because LIMIT is not guaranteed to apply before the lock function runs.

Partial index: "an index built over a subset of a table; the subset is defined by a conditional expression (called the predicate)"; Example 11.2 indexes only unbilled orders (`CREATE INDEX orders_unbilled_index ON orders (order_nr) WHERE billed is not true;`) because they are a small fraction yet the most-accessed rows — the canonical pattern for indexing only queued jobs.

INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE "guarantees an atomic INSERT or UPDATE outcome … even under high concurrency. This is also known as UPSERT"; for DO UPDATE a conflict_target must be provided; SET/WHERE can reference the existing row by table name and the proposed row via the special `excluded` table (e.g. `ON CONFLICT (did) DO UPDATE SET dname = EXCLUDED.dname`).

CURRENT_TIMESTAMP / now() / transaction_timestamp() "return the start time of the current transaction, their values do not change during the transaction"; statement_timestamp() returns the start of the current statement; "clock_timestamp() returns the actual current time, and therefore its value changes even within a single SQL statement."

"All timezone-aware dates and times are stored internally in UTC" (timestamp with time zone / timestamptz, a PostgreSQL abbreviation); bare `timestamp` is `timestamp without time zone` per the SQL standard, and for that type "PostgreSQL will silently ignore any time zone indication"; docs recommend date/time types containing both date and time when using time zones.

Kubernetes node heartbeats: two forms — updates to Node .status and Lease objects in kube-node-lease (Leases are lightweight, reducing load in large clusters). Defaults: kubelet updates .status on change or every 5 minutes ("much longer than the 40 second default timeout for unreachable nodes"); kubelet creates/updates its Lease every 10 seconds, retrying on failure with exponential backoff from 200 ms capped at 7 s; the node controller checks each node every 5 seconds (--node-monitor-period), sets Ready=Unknown when unreachable, and by default waits 5 minutes after Unknown before the first eviction.

Kubernetes Lease API: "every kubelet heartbeat is an update request to this Lease object, updating the spec.renewTime field for the Lease. The Kubernetes control plane uses the time stamp of this field to determine the availability of this Node."

Hadoop YARN Fair Scheduler: "Fair scheduling is a method of assigning resources to applications such that all apps get, on average, an equal share of resources over time… When there is a single app running, that app uses the entire cluster. When other apps are submitted, resources that free up are assigned to the new apps, so that each app eventually gets roughly the same amount of resources"; "this lets short apps finish in reasonable time while not starving long-lived apps"; priorities act as weights; optional guaranteed minimum shares, with excess split among other running apps.

Linux cgroup v2 resource-distribution models: Weights — "A parent's resource is distributed by adding up the weights of all active children and giving each the fraction matching the ratio of its weight against the sum", work-conserving ("only children which can make use of the resource at the moment participate"), range [1, 10000], default 100; Limits — "A child can only consume up to the configured amount of the resource. Limits can be over-committed". cpu.weight default "100"; cpu.max default "max 100000" ($MAX $PERIOD).

Dominant Resource Fairness (Ghodsi, Zaharia, Hindman, Konwinski, Shenker, Stoica; NSDI 2011): "a large number of algorithms have been proposed to implement (weighted) max-min fairness with various degrees of accuracy, such as round-robin, proportional resource sharing, and weighted fair queueing"; DRF is "a generalization of max-min fairness to multiple resource types" that "seeks to maximize the minimum dominant share across all users", is sharing-incentivizing, strategy-proof, envy-free and Pareto efficient, and "In the single resource case, DRF reduces to max-min fairness for that resource."

Kubernetes API Priority and Fairness: "Within a priority level, a fair-queuing algorithm prevents requests from different flows from starving each other"; each request is assigned to a flow by FlowSchema plus a flow distinguisher ("either the requesting user, the target resource's namespace, or nothing") and "the system attempts to give approximately equal weight to requests in different flows of the same priority level"; shuffle sharding insulates low-intensity flows from high-intensity ones.

Tailscale Serve identity headers: Tailscale-User-Login ("the requester's login name (for example, alice@example.com)"), Tailscale-User-Name (display name), Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic; "If Serve finds the following headers on an incoming request, it will remove them for security reasons, to avoid header spoofing"; headers are included only for tailnet traffic via Serve (Funnel traffic does not include them), "are not populated for traffic originating from tagged devices", ARE populated for external users who accepted a device share; "When you use the identity headers to authenticate to a backend service, it's best practice to only have the service listen on localhost." Example: `tailscale serve 3000` proxies to http://127.0.0.1:3000; flags --bg, --http=<port>, --https=<port> (default), --tcp=<port>, --set-path, --yes; HTTPS uses an automatically provisioned TLS certificate.
facts.version: KB as of 2026-08-22; CLI flags at https://tailscale.com/kb/1242/tailscale-serve

facts.statement: Tailscale CLI `tailscale whois ip[:port]` — "Get the machine and user associated with a Tailscale IP"; `--json` outputs JSON and must precede the address; output sections Machine (Name = machine name, ID, Addresses, AllowedIPs, Tags for tagged devices), User (Name = "the email address for the owner of the device", ID), Capabilities.

Tailscale LocalAPI: client/local.Client.WhoIs (comment: "API maturity: this is considered a stable API") issues GET /localapi/v0/whois?addr=<ip[:port]> and decodes apitype.WhoIsResponse{Node *tailcfg.Node, UserProfile *tailcfg.UserProfile, CapMap}; the handler (ipn/localapi serveWhoIsWithBackend) requires PermitRead (else 403 "whois access denied"), accepts addr as IP or IP:port (or nodekey:…), and returns 404 "no match for IP:port" when unknown.

On Linux tailscaled's unix socket is created world-accessible (safesocket socketPermissionsForOS returns 0666 when PlatformUsesPeerCreds, which is true for linux/darwin/freebsd/solaris/illumos; otherwise 0600) and ipnserver actor.Permissions grants read=true to any unix-socket client (`return true, !a.ci.IsReadonlyConn(operatorUID, …)`), so read-only LocalAPI calls such as whois/status work without root; write requires root or the configured operator user.

Userspace networking: "tailscaled functions as a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy which other processes in the container can connect through", enabled by passing `--tun=userspace-networking` to tailscaled before `tailscale up`; the official Docker image has TS_USERSPACE "Enabled by default. This is equivalent to tailscaled --tun=userspace-networking", TS_SERVE_CONFIG "Accepts a JSON file to programmatically configure Tailscale Serve and Tailscale Funnel", TS_SOCKET "Defaults to /var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock".
facts.version: KB as of 2026-08-22; Docker params at https://tailscale.com/docs/features/containers/docker/docker-params

facts.statement: In userspace mode tailscaled's netstack handles inbound traffic to the node's own Tailscale IPs (ProcessLocalIPs) and, for TCP to a Tailscale IP/port it does not itself serve, rewrites the dial target to the loopback address (`case isTailscaleIP: dialIP = ipv4Loopback`) and forwardTCP dials 127.0.0.1:<port> with a standard net.Dialer — i.e. the local backend receives a connection originated from the host's loopback, not from the peer's tailnet IP, so IP-based whois cannot identify the caller on a userspace-mode host.

Tailscale Serve (and therefore its identity headers) works while tailscaled runs with --tun=userspace-networking on a bare-metal Linux host (the hub). Implied by the official container image defaulting to userspace mode while exposing TS_SERVE_CONFIG, but not stated for non-container hosts in any KB page found.

PostgreSQL logging defaults: log_statement valid values none|ddl|mod|all, "The default is none"; log_min_duration_statement "-1 (the default) disables logging statement durations"; log_parameter_max_length "-1 (the default) allows bind parameters to be logged in full" (when statement logging is on); log_parameter_max_length_on_error "Zero (the default) disables including bind parameters in error messages"; log_connections default '' (disabled); log_disconnections default off; log_line_prefix default '%m [%p] '.

llama-server flags: `--log-prompts-dir PATH` "Log prompts to directory … only used for debugging, default: disabled"; `--slots, --no-slots` "expose slots monitoring endpoint (default: enabled)" (GET /slots returns per-slot processing state incl. sampling parameters); `--metrics` Prometheus endpoint "(default: disabled)"; `--log-disable`, `--log-file FNAME`, `--log-verbosity N` (default 3 = info).

"PostgreSQL is released under the PostgreSQL License, a liberal Open Source license, similar to the BSD or MIT licenses"; copyright "Portions Copyright © 1996-2026, The PostgreSQL Global Development Group; Portions Copyright © 1994, The Regents of the University of California".

The docker-library/postgres repository (Dockerfiles/entrypoint for the official image) is licensed MIT (GitHub license API spdx_id MIT); the image README's License section says "View license information for the software contained in this image" (→ PostgreSQL License) and notes the image also contains other software (e.g. Debian/Alpine base) under other licenses.
docker/compose latest release is v5.5.0 (published 2026-08-17); repository license Apache-2.0.
psycopg (Python PostgreSQL driver) latest tag 3.3.4; LICENSE.txt at that tag is GNU Lesser General Public License v3.0 (LGPL-3.0); psycopg-pool latest tag pool-3.3.1.
tailscale/tailscale latest release v1.102.3 (published 2026-08-20); repository license BSD-3-Clause.
Candidate Python API stack licenses: fastapi/fastapi latest release 0.141.1, MIT; encode/uvicorn latest release 0.52.4, BSD-3-Clause.

recommendations: Postgres compose project: its own directory with top-level `name: corvid-db` (no `version:`), image pinned to a full tag (`postgres:18.6-trixie`, or `18.6-alpine` if size matters), bind mount `/srv/corvid/pg:/var/lib/postgresql` (18+ location; NOT /var/lib/postgresql/data), `shm_size: 256mb`, `restart: unless-stopped`, POSTGRES_PASSWORD via env file kept out of git. Cite R06-F6, F7, F8, F10.

Resource caps for the DB container: use `deploy.resources.limits: {cpus: '1.0', memory: 1g, pids: 200}` plus `deploy.resources.reservations.memory` — verified to be honored by docker compose v5.5.0 (R06-F2); never set deploy `reservations.cpus` (swarm-only). Keep `mem_limit`/`cpus` out to avoid the must-be-consistent rule (R06-F3). Tune the cap after measuring; a GTX-970-era hub should protect llama-server's RAM.

Healthcheck: `test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U $POSTGRES_USER -d $POSTGRES_DB"]`, interval 10s, timeout 5s, retries 5, start_period 30s; coordinator uses `depends_on: db: {condition: service_healthy}` if in the same project, or its own readiness loop if in a separate project. Pass real -U/-d so health probes don't spam failed-auth log lines (R06-F4, F12).

Schema migrations as /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/*.sql only for the very first boot; everything after via `db/` migrations applied by the coordinator (initdb.d never re-runs and a failed script leaves a half-initialized dir) (R06-F9).

Network exposure: do NOT publish 5432 at all if the coordinator shares the Docker network; if it must be published, bind to the hub's tailnet IP only (`100.x.y.z:5432:5432`), never 0.0.0.0 — matches CLAUDE.md §5.6.

Queue claim query (one statement, no advisory locks): `UPDATE job SET state='running', claimed_by=$node, claimed_at=clock_timestamp(), lease_until=clock_timestamp()+interval '2 minutes' WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM job WHERE state='queued' AND (run_after IS NULL OR run_after<=now()) ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING *;` with partial index `CREATE INDEX job_queued_idx ON job (priority DESC, created_at) WHERE state='queued';` (R06-F15, F16, F20). Avoid OFFSET in claim queries (F16).

Wake-up without busy-polling: statement trigger `AFTER INSERT ON job … NOTIFY job_queued` with empty/key-only payload; workers LISTEN and also poll every ~5 s as a backstop (payload <8000 B, delivered only on commit) (R06-F18).

Lease/heartbeat for running jobs: `lease_until timestamptz` renewed by the executing agent; a reaper loop re-queues rows whose lease expired (`state='running' AND lease_until < now()`), bumping `attempt`. Use clock_timestamp() or client-side timestamps inside long transactions since now() is frozen at transaction start (R06-F22).

Roster schema: `node(node_id text PK, owner_login text, os text, arch text, caps jsonb, last_seen timestamptz, agent_version text, …)` written via `INSERT … ON CONFLICT (node_id) DO UPDATE SET last_seen=EXCLUDED.last_seen, caps=EXCLUDED.caps` (R06-F21); heartbeat every 10 s, node considered 'unreachable' after 40 s without a heartbeat, derived at read time (`CASE WHEN last_seen > now()-interval '40 seconds'`), never stored — mirrors Kubernetes Lease defaults (R06-F24, F25). Keep a separate append-only `heartbeat_log`/`job_run` table for the thank-you board, not the live row.
All time columns `timestamptz`, never bare `timestamp` (R06-F23).

Fair share with no quotas: at claim time pick the next job from the member with the fewest currently-running jobs (tie → oldest), i.e. per-member round-robin = max-min fairness; one member alone gets the whole pool, and a flood from one member cannot starve others (R06-F26, F28, F29). Put the same rule in front of llama-server (per-member FIFO lanes, round-robin dispatch into `--parallel` slots). Inside a host, express the co-op's share as weights (`cpu_shares`/cgroup cpu.weight) and reserve hard limits (`cpus`/cpu.max, `mem_limit`) for the OWNER's politeness caps (R06-F14, F27) — weights share, limits cap.

Identity for the API on the hub: coordinator listens on 127.0.0.1 only; expose it with `tailscale serve --bg <port>`; trust `Tailscale-User-Login` as the caller identity (Serve strips spoofed copies; only tailnet traffic gets headers); reject requests without the header (R06-F30). Do not rely on whois-by-source-IP on solarplexus: userspace netstack hands the backend a loopback connection (R06-F35). Keep `tailscale whois` / LocalAPI `/localapi/v0/whois` for kernel-mode nodes and for the agent's own CLI (R06-F31–F33).
Member devices must NOT be tagged (tags suppress identity headers); agents authenticate as the owner's login via the same headers, plus a `node_id` they generate locally (R06-F30).

Log policy: set `log_statement=none`, `log_min_duration_statement=-1`, `log_connections=''`, `log_disconnections=off` explicitly in the compose `command:` so defaults can't drift (R06-F37). Store only metadata in Postgres (who, which node, model name, token counts, durations, exit status); never prompt/completion text or job stdout. llama-server: `--no-slots`, never `--log-prompts-dir`, `--metrics` allowed (aggregate) (R06-F38). Write this as the docs/ 'what we log' page members read.

Credit rows to add to CLAUDE.md §4 in the same commit as the code: PostgreSQL (PostgreSQL License), postgres Docker Official Image (MIT Dockerfiles), Docker Compose (Apache-2.0), psycopg 3 (LGPL-3.0 — dynamic import from Python is fine), and note Tailscale Serve/whois usage under the existing Tailscale row; idea-credits for Hadoop Fair Scheduler, DRF, and Kubernetes leases.
Pin Postgres 18 (supported to 2030-11) unless the hub's Docker/kernel is old; plan `pg_upgrade --link` using the new /var/lib/postgresql layout (R06-F7, F11).
open_questions: Does `tailscale serve` (with identity headers) work on solarplexus while tailscaled runs in --tun=userspace-networking? Implied by the container image defaults (R06-F36) but unverified on bare metal — needs a 10-minute spike before the API design is frozen.

Same compose project or two? Putting coordinator + Postgres in one project gives `depends_on: service_healthy` for free; separate projects (as asked) need a named external network or a tailnet-bound port. Decide in the coordinator ADR.
Postgres major: 18 vs 17 on the hub — does the hub's Docker version/kernel support the 18 image cleanly, and who owns the bind-mount dir (uid 999 vs arbitrary --user)?

Agent identity: member-login headers (no tags) vs tagged machines with a shared secret — tags remove identity headers (R06-F30); what should the roster key on when one member owns several machines (node_id + owner_login?).

Fair-share granularity for inference: per request at the coordinator vs per token inside llama-server slots; does llama-server's own slot queue already behave acceptably at 6 users (measure before building).
Retention for the metadata-only logs: how long do job_run / heartbeat_log rows live, and is the contribution board fed from them or from a rollup table?
Do we want LISTEN/NOTIFY at all in v1, or is 5-second polling by ≤20 agents simply fine? (Probably fine; NOTIFY is an optimization.)
Ready-made Python queue libs on SKIP LOCKED exist; hand-rolled is ~30 lines. Confirm §7 non-goal reading: hand-roll here is acceptable because no scheduler is being invented.

Where does `tailscale whois` matter then? Kernel-mode nodes (laptops) can use source-IP whois for their local agent UI; confirm whether any API is served from a kernel-mode node or everything fronts through the hub.

verdicts.corrected_statement: The official postgres image supports running as a "(mostly) arbitrary" user via `--user` on `docker run` (docker-library/postgres#253; Alpine variants since #1018). Caveat (verbatim): "postgres doesn't care what UID it runs as (as long as the owner of PGDATA matches), but initdb does care (and needs the user to exist in /etc/passwd)" — e.g. `--user www-data` works but `--user 1000:1000` fails with "initdb: could not look up effective user ID 1000: user does not exist". The three documented workarounds are: (1) let the image use the nss_wrapper library to fake /etc/passwd (docker-library/postgres#448); (2) bind-mount the host's /etc/passwd read-only if the UID exists on the host: `docker run ... --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v /etc/passwd:/etc/passwd:ro -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=... postgres`; (3) initialize the data directory separately from the final runtime — run once as the default postgres user to initdb, stop it, `chown -R 1000:1000` the volume, then run with `--user 1000:1000`. Note: the Docker Hub page (hub.docker.com/_/postgres) is trimmed at the 25,000-char Hub limit and omits the workaround commands; the full text is in docker-library/docs postgres/content.md (master @ c4a9ba4).

The "Locking Clause" section contains the quoted sentences verbatim: "With SKIP LOCKED, any selected rows that cannot be immediately locked are skipped. Skipping locked rows provides an inconsistent view of the data, so this is not suitable for general purpose work, but can be used to avoid lock contention with multiple consumers accessing a queue-like table." The same section gives the general form "FOR lock_strength [ OF from_reference [, ...] ] [ NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED ]" with lock_strength one of UPDATE, NO KEY UPDATE, SHARE, KEY SHARE, and states "With NOWAIT, the statement reports an error, rather than waiting, if a selected row cannot be locked immediately." The synopsis grammar matches ("FOR { UPDATE | NO KEY UPDATE | SHARE | KEY SHARE } [ OF from_reference [, ...] ] [ NOWAIT | SKIP LOCKED ]"). Source is primary (official PostgreSQL docs) and current for PostgreSQL 18. Claim fully supported; only minor nuance omitted (NOWAIT/SKIP LOCKED apply to row-level locks only; the ROW SHARE table-level lock is still taken normally), which does not contradict the claim as stated.

Fetched https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html (title "PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: SELECT", page header "PostgreSQL 18.6 Documentation"), a primary source. The anchor id="SQL-FOR-UPDATE-SHARE" is present, and The Locking Clause section contains the sentence verbatim: "If a LIMIT is used, locking stops once enough rows have been returned to satisfy the limit (but note that rows skipped over by OFFSET will get locked)." The claim matches the cited source word-for-word for the stated version (PostgreSQL 18).

Fetched https://www.postgresql.org/docs/release/9.5.0/ (primary source, postgresql.org official release notes, release date 2016-01-07). Section E.26.3.3 "Queries" contains verbatim: "Add SELECT option SKIP LOCKED to skip locked rows (Thomas Munro)" / "This does not throw an error for locked rows like NOWAIT does." The quoted text, the version (9.5), the author attribution, and the section (Queries) all match the claim exactly. The only nit is that the dossier writes the section as "E.x.3.3" while the live page numbers it E.26.3.3; this is a placeholder, not an error of substance.

Fetched https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-notify.html (HTTP 200; page title "PostgreSQL: Documentation: 18: NOTIFY", so "current" resolves to PostgreSQL 18 as the claim states; primary source). All three quoted/paraphrased parts appear verbatim or near-verbatim: (1) Parameters > payload: "In the default configuration it must be shorter than 8000 bytes. (If binary data or large amounts of information need to be communicated, it's best to put it in a database table and send the key of the record.)" — exact match. (2) Description: "if a NOTIFY is executed inside a transaction, the notify events are not delivered until and unless the transaction is committed." — exact match. (3) Description: "a useful programming technique is to put the NOTIFY in a statement trigger that is triggered by table updates. In this way, notification happens automatically when the table is changed, and the application programmer cannot accidentally forget to do it." — the claim's "recommended technique" is a fair paraphrase of "useful programming technique". Only nit: the docs say "useful" rather than "recommended"; not material enough to refute.

Fetched both cited pages (HTTP 200; "current" resolves to docs/18/, i.e. PostgreSQL 18, matching the stated version). Both are primary (official postgresql.org documentation). Every element of the claim is supported verbatim: §13.3.5 says advisory locks "have application-defined meanings ... the system does not enforce their use"; session-level locks are "held until explicitly released or the session ends" and "do not honor transaction semantics"; transaction-level locks "are automatically released at the end of the transaction, and there is no explicit unlock operation"; and the warning text and SQL are exact — "especially in queries involving explicit ordering and LIMIT clauses ... SELECT pg_advisory_lock(id) FROM foo WHERE id > 12345 LIMIT 100; -- danger! ... the LIMIT is not guaranteed to be applied before the locking function is executed." §9.28.10 (Table 9.109) says resources are "identified either by a single 64-bit key value or two 32-bit key values", and pg_try_advisory_lock / pg_try_advisory_xact_lock "will either obtain the lock immediately and return true, or return false without waiting if the lock cannot be acquired immediately." No discrepancy found; claim stands as written for PostgreSQL 18.

Fetched https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-partial.html (page header: "Documentation -> PostgreSQL 18"; primary source, postgresql.org official docs). The definition is verbatim: "A partial index is an index built over a subset of a table; the subset is defined by a conditional expression (called the predicate of the partial index)." Example 11.2, titled "Setting up a Partial Index to Exclude Uninteresting Values", states: "If you have a table that contains both billed and unbilled orders, where the unbilled orders take up a small fraction of the total table and yet those are the most-accessed rows, you can improve performance by creating an index on just the unbilled rows," with the statement exactly as quoted: CREATE INDEX orders_unbilled_index ON orders (order_nr) WHERE billed is not true;. Version attribution (PostgreSQL 18) matches /current/ as of today. Caveat only: the closing phrase "the canonical pattern for indexing only queued jobs" is the dossier's own application/analogy; the source says nothing about job queues, but the factual content attributed to the source is accurate and the analogy (small, hot subset of rows) is consistent with the example's stated rationale.

missing: Reuse-vs-new vs Immich's Postgres (spec §6.1 R06 asked for the decision to be recorded): no fact on what image/version Immich's `immich-db` container pins (the vectorchord/pgvecto.rs-patched Postgres) or whether Immich's docs permit sharing its DB with other apps; record 'new, separate project' (or not) with the citation.

Hub placement facts absent: which disk/filesystem holds PGDATA on solarplexus (/ with 242 GB free vs /mnt/disk1|disk2 vs the mergerfs/FUSE pool — is a FUSE pool acceptable for a Postgres data dir?), the host path convention for the new compose project (where the media stack's compose files live, owner), bind-mount ownership (image default uid 999 vs `--user <unattended-uid>` per F13 so inspection/backups need no root), and a backup method/destination (pg_dump via `docker compose exec`, schedule, executor) — 'data dir disk' was a key question and backups are unaddressed.

Rights of the unattended user on solarplexus: is it in the `docker` group (root-equivalent — acceptable to the founder?), or is every `docker compose` step `executor: Opus (splx-root)`? Rootless Docker considered? This sets executor tags for the whole Phase 2 plan and is not in the facts.

Compose version actually installed on the hub: Docker is the Ubuntu `docker.io` package (29.1.3-0ubuntu3~24.04.2, R00-F9) and the compose plugin ships separately (`docker-compose-v2`). F2 verifies deploy.resources handling against docker/compose v5.5.0 source, not the hub's version; do F2, F4 `start_interval` (needs Engine ≥25 + recent compose) and F5 `bind.create_host_path` hold at `docker compose version` on solarplexus, or is upgrading compose a plan step?

Postgres port/publish decision and syntax: should Postgres be published at all (API in the same compose network → no `ports:`), or on `127.0.0.1:5432` / `<tailnet-ip>:5432` for Grafana (R07)/psql? Missing: compose `ports:` host-IP syntax (`[HOST_IP:]HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT`, long-form `host_ip:`) that the bind-target CI lint requires, and the constraint that binding a published port to the tailnet IP requires kernel-mode tailscaled (no interface IP in userspace mode).

Where the coordinator API runs — container in the same compose project vs host systemd unit (user unit needs linger per R00-F8; no uv on the hub) — is undecided and unsupported by facts for either path. Container path needs: bind-mount of the hub's socket (`/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock` per the R00 log, not F34's `/var/run/tailscale`), the `tailscale` CLI in the image or the raw LocalAPI HTTP contract (required Host header / `Sec-Tailscale` / 403 rules), how the API sees the peer's tailnet IP (`network_mode: host` vs bridge + published port), and whether solarplexus's policy rule `100 from <docker-net> → <vpn-table>` (R00-F3) pulls replies from a NEW compose bridge network into the VPN table and breaks tailnet→container traffic.

Identity conflict with ADR-0002: F30 says Serve identity headers are not populated for tagged devices, and whois on a tagged node returns no real user (the `tagged-devices` pseudo-user) — but ADR-0002 tags contributing member machines `tag:member`, so a member browsing from their own contributing laptop has no zero-login identity. Needs the fact (what `WhoIsResponse.UserProfile`/`Node.User` holds for a tagged node) and a resolution: untag member devices (ACL by user/group), per-member tags, or a coordinator-maintained node→owner table.

Identity mechanism for the API given ADR-0003's Caddy front door: Serve proxies only to localhost (F30) and listens on `<tailnet-ip>:443`/`:80` — the ports ADR-0003 gives Caddy. Does `tailscale serve --https=443` conflict with Caddy bound to the tailnet IP :443 in kernel mode? Is the chain Serve→Caddy(127.0.0.1)→apps (headers forwarded by Caddy) or Caddy→API with whois on `X-Forwarded-For` (trusted_proxies)? For the headers path: version pin (do `--http=<port>` and `Tailscale-User-*` exist in 1.98.4 vs 1.102.3 — spec demands 'with version pinned'), does `--http` work without HTTPS certs enabled on the tailnet (R00-D11 UNVERIFIED → S-05, still blocked), does `serve --bg` persist across tailscaled restarts/reboots, and who runs it (root/operator → `Opus (splx-root)`). Also state that Phase 2 assumes the kernel-mode hub (Phase 0 step 2) and what then holds for whois on direct connections (F35/F36 only cover userspace mode).

Which Tailscale node identifier is the roster primary key: `tailcfg.Node.StableID` (stable across re-auth/rename) vs `ID` vs `Name` (changes on rename) vs node key (rotates on re-auth/180-day expiry per ADR-0002)? F31/F32 list the fields but not their stability; a wrong pick duplicates nodes after a member re-authenticates.

Heartbeat interval and node-down threshold are not chosen: F24/F25 give Kubernetes' 10 s lease / 40 s timeout (4×), but Phase 2 acceptance needs 'N = 3 × the heartbeat interval chosen in R06'. State the recommended interval, the down threshold, the down-detection query (server-side `last_seen < now() - interval`, per F22), and the agent's retry/backoff on failure.

Roster/heartbeat schema is not proposed: latest-only upsert (F21) vs an append-only heartbeat/session history for the thank-you board (CLAUDE.md §3.4; ADR-0001 'contributions appear only as thanks') and, if history, its retention; representation of the opt-in capability report (`offers: none` default; JSONB vs columns); which fields the agent may report (caps, GPU, idle/battery state) — no fact supports these choices.

Queue mechanics beyond the lock clause (key question asked for the pattern): the canonical claim statement (`UPDATE jobs … WHERE id = (SELECT id … ORDER BY … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING *`), that the row lock lasts only for the transaction (long-running jobs need a `running` state + lease/heartbeat + reclaim rule when a node dies), psycopg3 transaction/autocommit semantics for holding vs releasing the lock, and LISTEN/NOTIFY consumption from psycopg3 (dedicated connection outside the pool).

Fair share is background only (F26–F29): no implementable rule for a friends-scale SQL queue (e.g. dequeue ordered by per-member running-job count then age = max-min in one query, no quota table), and nothing on inference-side contention — llama-server `--parallel`/`-np` slots, continuous batching, and what happens when all slots are busy (FIFO queue vs 503) — which is the only 'fair share' Phases 1–2 actually exercise. Also whether `/slots` (F38, enabled by default) exposes prompt text and should be disabled under the log policy.

Log-policy gaps: Postgres `log_min_error_statement` defaults to `error`, so a failing INSERT/UPDATE is logged with its full SQL text (literal values included) despite F37's `log_parameter_max_length_on_error=0` — needs a setting or parameters-only discipline; uvicorn/FastAPI access-log defaults (method+path+query string; `--no-access-log`); Docker `json-file` driver has no rotation by default (`logging.options.max-size/max-file`); retention window for metadata logs/heartbeat history; whether `Tailscale-User-Login` (an email) may be stored/logged (spec §3.8 forbids usernames in the repo; DB/log policy unstated).

Healthcheck false positive: pg_isready (F12) returns 0 during first-run initdb/init-script phase because the entrypoint's temporary server listens on the unix socket only, so `depends_on: condition: service_healthy` (F4) fires early and the dependent's first connection is reset when the temp server stops; usual fix is `pg_isready -h 127.0.0.1 -U … -d …` (TCP only with the real server) with `$$` env escaping in compose — not captured.

Concrete resource caps for hub services are not recommended: the Phase 2 spec must set `cpus:`/`mem_limit:`/`shm_size` for Postgres and the API on a 4-thread/16 GB hub also running Plex/Immich/Tdarr; F8/F14 give mechanics but no values, nothing on Postgres's 128 MB default `shared_buffers`/OOM behaviour under a small `mem_limit`, and no restart-policy recommendation (`unless-stopped`).

Secrets and migrations: where `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` lives (`.env` git-ignored; `POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE` supported by the image — not in F7) and how schema changes are applied after first init, since `/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` never re-runs (F9): `db/` migrations via `psql -f` through `docker compose exec`, a Python migrator, or a tool (needing its own §4 row).

Credit rows incomplete for `add-dependency`: F39–F44 give licenses but no authors (docker-library/postgres maintainers; Docker Inc. for Compose; Daniele Varrazzo/Psycopg Team; Sebastián Ramírez for FastAPI; Encode/Tom Christie for uvicorn) and no pinned image tag decision (17.x vs 18.x given F7's volume-path change; trixie vs alpine) — the §4 row needs all four columns at the pinned version.

research.dossier:
# R07 — Status page & identity

- **Depth:** full
- **Written:** 2026-08-22 by research agent (Fable) · **Verified:** 2026-08-22 (adversarial pass: pending)
- **Feeds:** Phase 2 spec (status page v0 at `:8092`, identity dependency of the coordinator API), ADR-0003 (Caddy front door), ADR-0002 (tags vs identity), S-05 (serve headers), R06 (heartbeat interval → node-down threshold)

## Purpose

Decide (a) Grafana vs a simple server-rendered page for the Phase 2 "live map of the co-op"; (b) how a member's Tailscale identity reaches CORVID web apps behind Caddy on the hub — and what changes when the hub's tailscaled runs in userspace mode, as solarplexus does today; (c) Caddy basics (`reverse_proxy`, `handle_path`, `bind`, `forward_auth`, `log`, config location) and licences; (d) what the live map must show per ADR-0001 and the Phase 2 acceptance numbers.

## Headline findings (the plan writer should read these first)

1. **Grafana is AGPL-3.0-only at v13.2.0** (with Apache-2.0 sub-packages); Grafana Labs' own Enterprise image is *proprietary* though "free". OSS Grafana has every panel the map needs (Stat, Gauge, Table, State timeline, Status history, Node graph, Canvas) and a built-in PostgreSQL data source — but it brings a second identity system (`[auth.proxy]`/anonymous), phone-home defaults (`reporting_enabled`, `check_for_updates` both true), binds `0.0.0.0` by default, and cannot guarantee "thanks, never ranks" (any table can be sorted). **Recommendation: status page v0 = a small server-rendered page** (FastAPI + Jinja2, optional htmx polling) reading Postgres; Grafana is a Phase 4 option for history/thank-you board if wanted.
2. **Identity, two mechanisms, both verified at tailscale v1.102.3 source:** `tailscale serve` injects `Tailscale-User-Login`, `Tailscale-User-Name`, `Tailscale-User-Profile-Pic` into proxied requests and *deletes* any incoming header of the same name (anti-spoof); headers are **not set for traffic from tagged nodes** and not set for Funnel. `tailscale whois ip[:port]` (CLI or LocalAPI `/localapi/v0/whois?addr=`) resolves a connecting address to node + user; on Linux any local user can call it (read-only LocalAPI over the 0666 unix socket `/var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock`).
3. **Userspace mode changes the wiring (matters today on solarplexus):** an inbound tailnet TCP connection to the node's own 100.x IP is rewritten by tailscaled's netstack to a dial of `127.0.0.1:<port>` on the host, and tailscaled registers that loopback `ip:srcport` → peer mapping so `whois 127.0.0.1:<srcport>` still resolves the peer. Consequences: services must listen on loopback (binding the tailnet IP is impossible — there is no `tailscale0`), they see `127.0.0.1` as the client, and whois must be called with **ip:port** (exactly what `tailscale nginx-auth` and Caddy's documented `forward_auth` Tailscale example pass via `Remote-Addr`/`Remote-Port`). In kernel mode (planned for solarplexus, finding 10) the app sees the real 100.x source and may bind the tailnet IP.
4. **Caddy is Apache-2.0 at v2.11.4.** `reverse_proxy` passes `Host` through and sets `X-Forwarded-For/Proto/Host` (ignoring incoming ones unless `trusted_proxies`); `header_up -Name` deletes a request header; `handle_path /x/*` = `handle` + `uri strip_prefix`; `bind <ip>` pins the listener; `forward_auth` grants on 2xx and `copy_headers A>B` renames identity headers for the app — Caddy's docs ship a Tailscale example for exactly this; `*.ts.net` certs come from local tailscaled (needs the tailnet HTTPS feature and `TS_PERMIT_CERT_UID=caddy`). Access logs redact Cookie/Authorization by default. Linux package: `/etc/caddy/Caddyfile`, `systemctl reload caddy`, admin API `localhost:2019` (the hub already listens on 2019 — R00-F7). `import conf.d/*` lets CORVID drop in its own route file.
5. **ADR-0002's `tag:member`** on machines members *also browse from* would strip serve identity headers and make whois return tags instead of a user. Tag only servers; keep members' consuming devices user-owned.
6. **HTTPS on the tailnet publishes `solarplexus.tail2990fc.ts.net`-style names to public CT logs** (Tailscale's own warning). `tailscale serve` has a `--http=<port>` flag (serve only, not funnel) and the HTTPS-feature prompt is only triggered for the HTTPS serve type (source), so plain-HTTP serve with identity headers is plausible — **S-05 must confirm at runtime**.
